questions.stem: This skin finding of pinpoint and blotchy red-purple lesions is the classic bleeding pattern seen in platelet disorders. What is the category of bleeding it represents?

explanation.summary: Petechiae, purpura, and ecchymoses on the skin are mucocutaneous bleeding, characteristic of platelet (primary hemostasis) disorders. Deep tissue and joint bleeding instead point to clotting factor deficiencies such as hemophilia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Petechiae, purpura, and ecchymoses on the skin are mucocutaneous bleeding, characteristic of platelet (primary hemostasis) disorders. Deep tissue and joint bleeding instead point to clotting factor deficiencies such as hemophilia.

questions.stem: This illustration shows the structure that forms within a blood vessel to stop bleeding. Which blood component aggregates first to initiate formation of this structure?

explanation.summary: The image depicts a hemostatic clot plugging a vessel. Clot formation begins with platelet adhesion and aggregation at the site of injury, which then triggers the fibrin mesh that stabilizes the clot.
explanation.whyCorrect: The image depicts a hemostatic clot plugging a vessel. Clot formation begins with platelet adhesion and aggregation at the site of injury, which then triggers the fibrin mesh that stabilizes the clot.

questions.stem: This bone marrow aspirate shows two large cells with abundant cytoplasm and multilobated nuclei. What is the normal function of these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They differentiate into mature red blood cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: They fragment to release platelets into the bloodstream

choices.label: C
choices.text: They produce antibodies against foreign antigens

choices.label: D
choices.text: They synthesize and secrete clotting factors

explanation.summary: The large cells are megakaryocytes. Platelets are produced when megakaryocytes in the bone marrow break down, releasing platelets into the blood stream; reduced megakaryocyte activity leads to decreased platelet production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The large cells are megakaryocytes. Platelets are produced when megakaryocytes in the bone marrow break down, releasing platelets into the blood stream; reduced megakaryocyte activity leads to decreased platelet production.

questions.stem: This peripheral blood smear shows a dense aggregate of platelets among the red cells. What artifact does this finding most likely produce on an automated complete blood count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A falsely elevated mean corpuscular volume

choices.label: B
choices.text: A falsely elevated white blood cell count

explanation.summary: Platelet clumping (agglutination) causes automated analyzers to undercount platelets, producing pseudothrombocytopenia. Redrawing in a citrate tube gives an accurate count; this must be excluded before working up true thrombocytopenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Platelet clumping (agglutination) causes automated analyzers to undercount platelets, producing pseudothrombocytopenia. Redrawing in a citrate tube gives an accurate count; this must be excluded before working up true thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: This peripheral blood smear (circled cells) shows fragmented red blood cells. The presence of these fragments most strongly implies which underlying process?

explanation.summary: The fragmented red cells are schistocytes, which imply microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) such as TTP, HUS, or DIC, where red cells are sheared as they pass through microthrombi in small vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: The fragmented red cells are schistocytes, which imply microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) such as TTP, HUS, or DIC, where red cells are sheared as they pass through microthrombi in small vessels.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with a low platelet count has the skin lesions shown. The multiple small red-purple spots do not blanch with pressure. What best explains their appearance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extravasation of blood from small vessels into the skin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Proliferation of abnormal dermal blood vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deposition of hemosiderin from chronic venous stasis

explanation.summary: The nonblanching red-purple macules are petechiae and purpura, caused by extravasation of blood from small vessels into the skin due to insufficient platelets. Blanching lesions like telangiectasias are due to vessel dilation, not bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: The nonblanching red-purple macules are petechiae and purpura, caused by extravasation of blood from small vessels into the skin due to insufficient platelets. Blanching lesions like telangiectasias are due to vessel dilation, not bleeding.

questions.stem: A patient with immune thrombocytopenia has the skin findings shown here (pinpoint red-purple spots on the ankle, left; a larger flat purplish bruise on the thigh, right). What is the direct underlying cause of these lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Occlusion of dermal vessels by platelet-rich microthrombi

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immune-complex vasculitis inflaming the small dermal vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased capillary fragility from vitamin C deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bleeding into the skin from a reduced platelet count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deficiency of clotting factor VIII causing deep-tissue hemorrhage

explanation.summary: The small pinpoint lesions are petechiae and the larger flat purple lesions are purpura/bruising. In ITP the platelet count falls so low that spontaneous bleeding from small dermal vessels leaks into the skin. There is no vessel occlusion, clotting-factor defect, vasculitis, or scurvy; the abnormality is purely a quantitative platelet deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The small pinpoint lesions are petechiae and the larger flat purple lesions are purpura/bruising. In ITP the platelet count falls so low that spontaneous bleeding from small dermal vessels leaks into the skin. There is no vessel occlusion, clotting-factor defect, vasculitis, or scurvy; the abnormality is purely a quantitative platelet deficiency.

questions.stem: This schematic shows how IgG antiplatelet antibodies coat platelets, which are then bound by macrophage Fc receptors and phagocytosed. Based on this mechanism, why are platelet transfusions generally ineffective in ITP?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The donor platelets are permanently sequestered and stored intact within the liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: The transfused platelets are also coated by antibody and are rapidly cleared

choices.label: C
choices.text: The infused platelets suppress the patient's own megakaryocyte production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transfused platelets provoke a severe anaphylactic transfusion reaction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Antibodies consume the transfused platelets' clotting factors before they can function

explanation.summary: The diagram shows opsonization of platelets by IgG and their destruction by macrophages via Fc receptors in the spleen. Any transfused platelets are opsonized by the same circulating antibody and destroyed just as fast as the patient's own, so transfusion gives only a fleeting rise and is reserved for severe, actively bleeding patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagram shows opsonization of platelets by IgG and their destruction by macrophages via Fc receptors in the spleen. Any transfused platelets are opsonized by the same circulating antibody and destroyed just as fast as the patient's own, so transfusion gives only a fleeting rise and is reserved for severe, actively bleeding patients.

questions.stem: This peripheral blood smear is marked with colored arrows pointing to abnormal cellular elements among the red cells. What do the arrowed structures most likely represent?

explanation.summary: Morphology assessment on a blood smear can reveal hereditary platelet disorders such as those producing abnormally large (giant) platelets. The arrows here indicate giant platelets among normal red cells, an abnormality detectable only by manual microscopic review.
explanation.whyCorrect: Morphology assessment on a blood smear can reveal hereditary platelet disorders such as those producing abnormally large (giant) platelets. The arrows here indicate giant platelets among normal red cells, an abnormality detectable only by manual microscopic review.

questions.stem: These platelet aggregation tracings show normal aggregation curves in response to ADP, adrenaline, and collagen, but an essentially flat (absent) response to ristocetin. Which category of disorder does this pattern best suggest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A defect in the vWF-GPIb adhesion pathway

explanation.summary: An isolated lack of response to ristocetin with preserved responses to ADP, adrenaline, and collagen points to a problem in the vWF-GPIb axis, seen in both von Willebrand disease (deficient/abnormal vWF) and Bernard-Soulier syndrome (deficient GPIb receptor).
explanation.whyCorrect: An isolated lack of response to ristocetin with preserved responses to ADP, adrenaline, and collagen points to a problem in the vWF-GPIb axis, seen in both von Willebrand disease (deficient/abnormal vWF) and Bernard-Soulier syndrome (deficient GPIb receptor).

questions.stem: This schematic shows platelets adhering to a damaged vessel wall via several labeled surface glycoprotein receptors and their ligands. A deficiency of which labeled receptor is responsible for Bernard-Soulier syndrome?

explanation.summary: GPIb is the platelet receptor that binds von Willebrand factor to mediate initial adhesion. In Bernard-Soulier syndrome platelets lack normal GPIb, so they cannot bind vWF and fail to aggregate in response to ristocetin despite normal responses to other agonists.
explanation.whyCorrect: GPIb is the platelet receptor that binds von Willebrand factor to mediate initial adhesion. In Bernard-Soulier syndrome platelets lack normal GPIb, so they cannot bind vWF and fail to aggregate in response to ristocetin despite normal responses to other agonists.

questions.stem: The fragmented red cells highlighted in this peripheral blood smear are specific for which process?

explanation.summary: These cells never appear in normal or artifactual smears; their presence indicates mechanical red-cell fragmentation from intravascular microthrombi, i.e., MAHA.
explanation.whyCorrect: These cells never appear in normal or artifactual smears; their presence indicates mechanical red-cell fragmentation from intravascular microthrombi, i.e., MAHA.

questions.stem: The labeled cells in this smear (including helmet cells and triangulocytes alongside intact red cells) point to which underlying pathology?

explanation.summary: Helmet cells and triangulocytes are morphologic subtypes of schistocytes, formed when red cells are cut passing through fibrin/platelet microthrombi in small vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Helmet cells and triangulocytes are morphologic subtypes of schistocytes, formed when red cells are cut passing through fibrin/platelet microthrombi in small vessels.

questions.stem: A patient with thrombotic microangiopathy has these skin findings. What is the most likely underlying cause?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased vascular fragility from vitamin C deficiency

explanation.summary: The petechiae and purpura pictured result from low platelet counts (consumed in microthrombi), which cause bleeding into the skin and oozing from small vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: The petechiae and purpura pictured result from low platelet counts (consumed in microthrombi), which cause bleeding into the skin and oozing from small vessels.

questions.stem: This diagram shows the normal enzymatic cleavage of ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers at the endothelium. Loss of this depicted function would most likely cause which disease?

explanation.summary: The enzyme shown normally cleaves ultra-large vWF multimers; its deficiency leaves these sticky multimers uncleaved, causing platelet-rich microthrombi characteristic of TTP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The enzyme shown normally cleaves ultra-large vWF multimers; its deficiency leaves these sticky multimers uncleaved, causing platelet-rich microthrombi characteristic of TTP.

questions.stem: The vessel depicted shows uncleaved ultra-large multimers trapping platelets into thrombi. As red cells are sheared passing these thrombi, which type of anemia develops?

explanation.summary: The platelet-vWF thrombi mechanically fragment passing erythrocytes, producing the microangiopathic hemolytic anemia seen in TTP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The platelet-vWF thrombi mechanically fragment passing erythrocytes, producing the microangiopathic hemolytic anemia seen in TTP.

questions.stem: This schematic shows a red cell contacting an intravascular thrombus and being cut as it passes. This mechanism is the basis of which finding in thrombotic microangiopathy?

explanation.summary: The thrombus acts like a blade, shearing intact erythrocytes into fragmented cells; this intravascular mechanical hemolysis defines microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thrombus acts like a blade, shearing intact erythrocytes into fragmented cells; this intravascular mechanical hemolysis defines microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

questions.stem: This photograph shows tissue specimens embedded in solid wax cassettes in preparation for microscopic examination. What is the primary purpose of embedding the tissue in these blocks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To stain the tissue with hematoxylin and eosin

choices.label: B
choices.text: To provide a firm supporting medium

choices.label: C
choices.text: To keep the cells alive for flow cytometry

choices.label: D
choices.text: To lyse the red blood cells before analysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: To amplify the tissue's DNA for molecular testing

explanation.summary: These are formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) blocks. The paraffin provides a firm medium that supports the fixed tissue so a microtome can slice it into thin sections for staining and microscopy. FFPE blocks also preserve morphology and can be stored for years.
explanation.whyCorrect: These are formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) blocks. The paraffin provides a firm medium that supports the fixed tissue so a microtome can slice it into thin sections for staining and microscopy. FFPE blocks also preserve morphology and can be stored for years.

questions.stem: In this stained section, many tumor nuclei display a brown chromogen while others remain blue. What does the brown signal indicate about the positively stained cells?

choices.label: D
choices.text: They express the specific target antigen

explanation.summary: This is an immunohistochemical (IHC) stain: a labeled antibody binds its target antigen, and a chromogen deposits brown color wherever the antigen is present. Brown-positive nuclei therefore express the specific protein being tested, which helps classify the tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is an immunohistochemical (IHC) stain: a labeled antibody binds its target antigen, and a chromogen deposits brown color wherever the antigen is present. Brown-positive nuclei therefore express the specific protein being tested, which helps classify the tumor.

questions.stem: In this image, interphase nuclei are counterstained blue and a chromosome-specific fluorescent probe appears as bright green signals. Finding three green signals per nucleus, rather than the expected two, indicates what?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An extra copy of that chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: A deletion of that chromosome region

explanation.summary: This is fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Each probe signal marks one copy of the targeted chromosome; three signals instead of two means an extra copy is present (trisomy). Because FISH uses specific probes, you must know which chromosome to interrogate.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Each probe signal marks one copy of the targeted chromosome; three signals instead of two means an extra copy is present (trisomy). Because FISH uses specific probes, you must know which chromosome to interrogate.

questions.stem: This flowchart organizes hematopoietic neoplasms into a branching hierarchy. What single feature does the WHO classification use at the FIRST branch point to divide these neoplasms into their two major groups?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lineage/cell of origin (myeloid vs lymphoid)

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rapidity of clinical progression (acute vs chronic)

choices.label: E
choices.text: The anatomic site of the tumor

explanation.summary: The WHO system first separates neoplasms by the cell of origin, distinguishing those arising from the myeloid stem cell line from those arising from the lymphoid line. Subsequent branches then subclassify within each group.
explanation.whyCorrect: The WHO system first separates neoplasms by the cell of origin, distinguishing those arising from the myeloid stem cell line from those arising from the lymphoid line. Subsequent branches then subclassify within each group.

questions.stem: This H&E field (arrow) shows a gigantic cell with two mirror-image nuclei, each containing a single prominent nucleolus, giving an 'owl-eye' appearance. Identification of this cell is diagnostic of which malignancy?

explanation.summary: The binucleate 'owl-eye' cell is a Reed-Sternberg cell, the defining feature of Hodgkin lymphoma. Although derived from B cells, these cells have lost their characteristic B-cell expression pattern, which is why Hodgkin lymphoma is classified separately from the B-cell neoplasms.
explanation.whyCorrect: The binucleate 'owl-eye' cell is a Reed-Sternberg cell, the defining feature of Hodgkin lymphoma. Although derived from B cells, these cells have lost their characteristic B-cell expression pattern, which is why Hodgkin lymphoma is classified separately from the B-cell neoplasms.

questions.stem: This schematic traces how a single precursor at the top of the hierarchy gives rise to every mature blood cell, split into myeloid and lymphoid lines. Malignant transformation of that precursor produces myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms. In which anatomic site does this precursor normally reside and begin differentiation?

explanation.summary: The single precursor at the apex is the hematopoietic stem cell, which resides in the bone marrow. Early differentiation into both the myeloid and lymphoid lineages occurs there before mature cells are released into the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: The single precursor at the apex is the hematopoietic stem cell, which resides in the bone marrow. Early differentiation into both the myeloid and lymphoid lineages occurs there before mature cells are released into the blood.

questions.stem: This graph plots the logarithm of tumor cell number against time during chemotherapy, showing sawtooth reductions with each treatment. What core principle of tumor kinetics does this curve illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single dose can eradicate all tumor cells if the dose is high enough

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each dose kills a constant absolute number of tumor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tumor regrowth between doses is impossible once treatment starts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tumor cells stop dividing entirely once therapy begins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each dose kills a constant fraction of tumor cells

explanation.summary: The plot depicts the log-cell kill hypothesis: because chemotherapy follows first-order kinetics, each cycle destroys a fixed proportion of remaining cells, so tumor burden falls logarithmically and multiple cycles are required to reach a clinically undetectable level.
explanation.whyCorrect: The plot depicts the log-cell kill hypothesis: because chemotherapy follows first-order kinetics, each cycle destroys a fixed proportion of remaining cells, so tumor burden falls logarithmically and multiple cycles are required to reach a clinically undetectable level.

questions.stem: This step-wise graph shows tumor cell count dropping by an equal proportion after each labeled 'X Dose'. What does the repeated 'constant fraction of cell kill' bracket demonstrate about why cure requires many cycles?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each dose becomes progressively more potent as tumor burden falls

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single dose reduces the tumor to zero cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Later doses kill a larger absolute number of cells than early doses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each identical dose eliminates the same percentage of surviving cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor becomes resistant after the first dose, halting further kill

explanation.summary: Because a fixed fraction is killed each cycle, the number of cells destroyed decreases as the population shrinks, meaning several cycles are needed to drive the count low enough for the immune system or other therapy to clear residual disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because a fixed fraction is killed each cycle, the number of cells destroyed decreases as the population shrinks, meaning several cycles are needed to drive the count low enough for the immune system or other therapy to clear residual disease.
